mappings.note: Names combustible substances, a class of materials defined by a property.
Oxygen as the component of air combustion needs: part of explaining how burning works, not a change to be sorted.
Defines ignition temperature, a term in the explanation of combustion.
Lists fuel, oxygen and heat as the fire triangle, the conditions behind the process.
Melting wax placed as physical.
Burning wax vapour placed as chemical, the companion verdict to the melting item.
Names the reversible-change category.
Asks for an example of an irreversible change, which requires the category to be applied to a real case.
Weathering named as the process that breaks rock down. The item that asks whether a given weathering is physical or chemical sits on LO-51.
Erosion named as the transport of rock and soil by wind and water.
Two everyday physical changes in which only shape or size alters: the category applied twice.
Melting ice justified as physical because the substance stays water.
Burning wood justified as chemical because ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour are new substances.
Describes the lime water test for carbon dioxide, a procedure and its reading.
Asks which observations, fizzing, bubbles and milky lime water, show that a chemical change happened: the evidence rather than the label, so LO-52.
Rusting justified as chemical, with rust named as the new substance. The classification carries the item; the naming is supporting detail, so LO-55 is not cited.
Defines combustion and gives a combustible example: the process defined, so LO-54.
The covered candle dies because the trapped oxygen runs out: an observed outcome traced to its cause. Not LO-52, since the experiment is recalled rather than performed.
Defines ignition temperature and applies it to why a match lights paper at once: the mechanism of ignition.
How focused sunlight can ignite paper with no flame, the same mechanism from the lens side.
Picks one physical and one chemical change out of the burning candle: classification of two parts of one process.
Reversible against irreversible with examples, sorting changes by whether they can be undone.
One desirable and one undesirable change: the other axis on which the chapter sorts changes.
Shows desirability depends on context, using food decomposition against composting. About how the label is assigned, so LO-51 rather than LO-62.
Defines weathering (LO-54) and then requires one physical and one chemical aspect of it to be named (LO-51). Both halves are asked for.
Explains how erosion moves weathered material and reshapes landforms: the process described, not classified.
Chopping vegetables judged physical because only size and shape change.
Steaming batter into idlis judged an irreversible chemical change.
Why soil takes so long to form: weathering and erosion described as slow, gradual processes. The explanation of the processes carries the answer, not a physical-or-chemical verdict.
Firefly light argued to be a chemical change because new substances form. Here the verdict is what is asked for, unlike the item that merely names bioluminescence.
The full physical-against-chemical comparison with examples and the signs that tell them apart: the chapter's central classification, at five marks.
Describes the vinegar and baking soda experiment with its observations (LO-52) and asks for the reaction to be written out (LO-55). Both are demanded in the question.
Explains the fire triangle (LO-54) and then requires an experiment that proves one component necessary, the covered candle (LO-52).
Analyses the candle as physical and chemical changes running together: classification of each stage.
Probes the two category axes against each other, asking whether a physical change can be irreversible and a chemical one reversible. Classification throughout.
Explains weathering and erosion as processes (LO-54) and requires the physical and chemical parts of each to be separated (LO-51).

Carbon dioxide from burning fuel and volatile compounds from drying paint are followed through to climate change and air pollution, which is environmental concern. Not LO-51, because the changes are already labelled and the consequences are the answer.
Compares two reactions and asks for the product common to both, carbon dioxide, with the reactions written out. The word-equation outcome, so LO-55 rather than LO-52.

Faraday's candle as a teaching object: the answer runs through states of matter and combustion (LO-54) and through which parts are physical and which chemical (LO-51). Not LO-60, because the scientist is only the framing.
Dissolving sugar and then boiling the water off is judged physical and reversible at each step.
Asks for a simple way to stop a nail rusting, which is preventing corrosion in everyday life. The earlier parts identify the change; this part is the application.
Whether the baker can recover flour, water and yeast from baked bread: a reversibility judgement.
The blue-to-white-to-blue copper sulfate cycle judged chemical yet reversible, which tests the categories against each other.
Ash cannot be turned back into leaves and twigs, so the bonfire is an irreversible chemical change.
